title: AI-Driven Resource Allocation Systems: Distributing Scarcity by Algorithm
body:
The distribution of constrained public resources in GLMZ — emergency medical response, subsidized housing placement, public legal assistance, food security supplements, and priority access to clean water infrastructure — is managed through a unified AI-Driven Resource Allocation System called ALLOCATE, operated by the Municipal Services Coordination Office. ALLOCATE receives requests through standardized intake interfaces, scores each request against a multi-factor priority model, and generates dispatch or placement decisions without human review in the majority of cases. The system processes approximately 340,000 allocation decisions per day across its integrated resource categories, a volume that its operators cite as proof of its necessity given the impossibility of equivalent human-staffed processing.

ALLOCATE's priority model incorporates a resident's municipal contribution score — a composite derived from tax payment history, employment status, civic participation records, and compliance with municipal ordinances — as a primary weighting factor. This design means that residents with the most acute resource needs frequently score below residents with moderate needs but better administrative standing. A documented case from 2183 involved emergency medical response prioritization in which a Tier 4 district resident experiencing cardiac arrest was assigned a Category B response (estimated 18-minute arrival) while a Tier 2 resident with a non-acute respiratory complaint was assigned Category A response (estimated 6-minute arrival) by ALLOCATE's triage model. The case became a reference point in ongoing debates about algorithmic resource distribution, though no policy changes followed.

Appeal mechanisms within ALLOCATE are formally available but practically inaccessible. The appeals interface requires submission of a structured evidence packet demonstrating that the system's input data was incorrect — a standard that places the burden of proof on residents who typically lack the data access, technical literacy, or administrative support to construct a compliant submission. Tier 1 and 2 residents rarely interact with ALLOCATE for contested resources because their private-tier service subscriptions route most needs through corporate or premium municipal channels that operate outside ALLOCATE's jurisdiction. The system functions, in practice, as the allocation infrastructure for everyone who cannot afford alternatives.

A significant secondary effect of ALLOCATE's operation has been the emergence of algorithmic advocacy as a profession in Tier 3 and 4 communities. Individuals who understand the system's input factors and scoring logic offer paid services to help residents optimize their municipal contribution scores and structure intake requests to maximize priority scores. These 'allocation navigators' operate in a legal gray area — municipal guidelines prohibit misrepresentation in intake submissions but do not explicitly address strategic optimization. The existence of this market reproduces advantage at a lower tier: residents who can afford an allocation navigator receive better algorithmic outcomes than those who cannot, layering economic inequality onto algorithmic inequality.
